column15: AI has the power to make education more accessible to a much larger population of people. In this regard it is quite helpful, as a larger number of students + students with disabilities that limit their access to in-person interactions can get 1-on-1 help. However, this help likely will not be as high quality as actual help from an educated human thinker, who is able to form new ideas and think critically (whereas LLMs are only following patterns and repeating information in different ways). Still, simple guidance from an LLM can be helpful in the case of tutoring, where expertise in the field might not be required from a tutor in that context. However, I am worried that LLMs do more harm than good in education as they are used not as a helping tool but as a shortcut by many students. It takes a lot of self-discipline to use AI in a productive way rather than just getting answers and inputting it into the homework. In the modern-day education system where students are largely rewarded for accurate results rather than critical thinking (it is much harder to test for proof of a thinking process, especially when a class is large in numbers), it is likely that many will use AI to get answers for homework assignments and even online exams. This discourages independent thinking, but also creates a false sense of trust with online sources that are not cited strongly. An LLM could very easily give an incorrect answer to a question, but present it with such confidence that the average user has little reason to doubt it, unless they are entering this interaction with the knowledge and mindset that the AI can give incorrect information and needs to be cross-checked / verified. All in all, I am worried that misuse of LLMs (not in the legal or technical sense, but rather in terms of integrity in academia) will harm the development of critical and independent thinking at the K-12 and undergraduate level of those who use it, and stunt the writing and other academic skill development of many students.
